# Does Medicare Cover Cataract Surgery? | Dr. Robert Weinstock, Largo FL

Source: https://proposals.localairegistry.com/weinstock/articles/does-medicare-cover-cataract-surgery/
Updated: 2026-11-19

Insurance

# What Medicare Covers for Cataract Surgery

Medicare covers medically necessary cataract surgery, but not every lens or upgrade. Here's what's included, what you may pay, and the questions to ask before surgery.

**By[Robert J. Weinstock, MD](https://proposals.localairegistry.com/weinstock/dr-robert-weinstock/)**Board-certified cataract & refractive surgeon · Largo, FL

**Published** November 17, 2026**Medically reviewed** November 17, 20266 min read

Stock photo.

**On this page**

  1. What Medicare covers
  2. What you may pay
  3. Premium lenses and upgrades
  4. If you have Medicare Advantage
  5. Glasses after cataract surgery
  6. Questions to ask before surgery
  7. FAQ
  8. Sources

**Key takeaways**

  * Medicare Part B may cover cataract surgery that implants a conventional intraocular lens.
  * After the Part B deductible, you generally pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount; a Medigap policy can help with that share.
  * Premium lenses that also correct astigmatism or near vision cost extra, and Medicare must always let you choose a standard lens.
  * After each covered cataract surgery with a lens implant, Part B covers one pair of standard eyeglasses or one set of contacts.

## What Medicare covers

Medicare Part B (Medical Insurance) may cover cataract surgery that implants a conventional intraocular lens.1 Coverage applies when your doctor determines surgery is medically necessary, typically because the cataract is affecting your daily life.2

Cataract surgery removes the cloudy natural lens and, in most cases, replaces it with a clear artificial lens.1

## What you may pay

For Original Medicare, after you meet the Part B deductible, you generally pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount.2 If you have a Medicare Supplement (Medigap) policy, it can cover all or part of that 20% coinsurance.3

Costs vary by where surgery is performed. Medicare's online [procedure price lookup](https://www.medicare.gov/procedure-price-lookup/) can give you an estimate, and our team will walk you through your own numbers before surgery.

Questions about your own eyes?

Book a consultation with Dr. Weinstock in Largo.

[Book a Consultation](https://proposals.localairegistry.com/weinstock/#contact)

## Premium lenses and upgrades

Medicare pays for what it takes to restore functional vision, which is surgery with a conventional lens. If you choose a lens that also corrects astigmatism or reduces your need for reading glasses, you can pay the difference for the premium portion.4

Two protections are worth knowing. Medicare patients must always be able to choose the standard lens, and a surgeon cannot require a premium lens as a condition of surgery.4

"A premium lens is a choice, never a requirement. We show patients exactly what each option does and what it costs, in writing, before anything is scheduled."

DR. ROBERT J. WEINSTOCK · DRAFT QUOTE FOR DR. WEINSTOCK'S APPROVAL

## If you have Medicare Advantage

Medicare Advantage plans must provide at least the same coverage as Original Medicare, which includes cataract surgery with a standard lens.5 Some plans add vision benefits. Advantage plans may require precertification before a practice can bill you for a premium lens upgrade, so we check with your plan in advance.6

## Glasses after cataract surgery

Medicare usually does not cover eyeglasses or contact lenses. The exception: after each cataract surgery that implants an intraocular lens, Part B covers one pair of eyeglasses with standard frames or one set of contact lenses.2 They must come from a supplier enrolled in Medicare.5

## Questions to ask before surgery

  * Is my surgery considered medically necessary, and is my lens choice covered?
  * What will I pay for the surgeon, the surgery center and any lens upgrade?
  * Does my Medicare Advantage plan require approval before surgery?
  * Which lens fits my eyes and lifestyle, and what does each option do differently?

Not sure you need surgery yet? Start with [the 7 signs it may be time for cataract surgery](https://proposals.localairegistry.com/weinstock/articles/signs-you-need-cataract-surgery/).

## Frequently asked questions

Does Medicare cover laser cataract surgery?

Medicare covers medically necessary cataract surgery. Some laser steps used for extra refractive benefits, such as correcting astigmatism, can carry an added cost. Ask for a written quote before surgery.

Does Medicare pay for both eyes?

Medicare covers cataract surgery for each eye when surgery is medically necessary for that eye. Most patients have the eyes done on separate days.

Will Medicare pay for my glasses after surgery?

After each cataract surgery that implants a lens, Part B covers one pair of eyeglasses with standard frames or one set of contacts from a Medicare-enrolled supplier.

Can I choose a premium lens with Medicare?

Yes. You can choose a premium lens and pay the difference for the premium portion, but you can always choose the standard lens that Medicare covers.

## Sources

  2. FedRateCalc. Does Medicare cover cataract surgery? (quoting Medicare.gov coverage pages). <https://fedratecalc.com/does-medicare-cover-cataract-surgery/>
  3. AARP. Does Medicare cover cataract surgery? <https://www.aarp.org/medicare/faq/does-medicare-cover-cataract-surgery/>

# LASIK vs. EVO ICL: Which Is Right for You? | Dr. Robert Weinstock, Largo FL

Source: https://proposals.localairegistry.com/weinstock/articles/lasik-vs-evo-icl/
Updated: 2026-11-19

Vision Correction

# LASIK vs. EVO ICL: How to Know Which Fits You

Both can free you from glasses and contacts, but they work in very different ways. Here's how to tell which one fits your eyes, your prescription and your life.

**By[Robert J. Weinstock, MD](https://proposals.localairegistry.com/weinstock/dr-robert-weinstock/)**Board-certified cataract & refractive surgeon · Largo, FL

**Published** November 17, 2026**Medically reviewed** November 17, 20267 min read

Stock photo.

**On this page**

  1. How each procedure works
  2. LASIK and EVO ICL side by side
  3. Who tends to fit LASIK
  4. Who tends to fit EVO ICL
  5. What if you're over 45?
  6. Questions to ask your surgeon
  7. FAQ
  8. Sources

**Key takeaways**

  * LASIK uses a laser to reshape the cornea and is FDA approved to treat nearsightedness, farsightedness and astigmatism.
  * EVO ICL is a thin lens placed inside the eye, behind the iris, without removing corneal tissue.
  * EVO ICL is often considered for higher prescriptions, thinner corneas or dry eye concerns.
  * Neither procedure prevents the need for reading glasses as you age; lens-based options may fit better after about 45.

## How each procedure works

**LASIK** uses a laser to reshape the cornea, the clear front window of the eye, so light focuses correctly. LASIK has been approved by the FDA to treat nearsightedness, farsightedness and astigmatism.1

**EVO ICL** (Implantable Collamer Lens) is a thin lens placed inside the eye, behind the iris, in front of your natural lens. Unlike LASIK, it corrects vision without removing corneal tissue.2 Because your natural lens stays in place, the approach is described as reversible and keeps future treatment options open.3

The FDA approved the EVO ICL in the United States on March 25, 2022, for correcting nearsightedness and nearsightedness with astigmatism.4 Earlier versions of the lens required a small laser opening in the iris before surgery; the EVO design does not.5

## LASIK and EVO ICL side by side

| LASIK| EVO ICL  
---|---|---  
How it works| Laser reshapes the cornea| Thin lens placed behind the iris  
Corneal tissue removed| Yes| No  
Reversible| No| The lens can be removed  
Often a good fit for| Stable prescriptions and healthy corneas| Higher prescriptions, thinner corneas or dry eye concerns  
Treats reading vision with age| No| No  
  
The right choice depends on measurements only a full exam can provide, including your prescription, corneal thickness and shape, and the space inside your eye.

Questions about your own eyes?

Book a consultation with Dr. Weinstock in Largo.

[Book a Consultation](https://proposals.localairegistry.com/weinstock/#contact)

## Who tends to fit LASIK

LASIK is often a strong option for adults whose prescription has been stable and whose corneas are healthy and thick enough to reshape. A thorough baseline evaluation decides whether you are a good candidate.6

Dry eye matters. The FDA notes that existing dry eye can get worse after LASIK, and some people develop dry eye as a result of surgery, so you should be screened before treatment.7

## Who tends to fit EVO ICL

EVO ICL is often considered when LASIK is not the best fit: higher amounts of nearsightedness, corneas that are thin or irregular, or dry eye that makes corneal surgery less appealing. At FDA approval it was indicated for adults 21 to 45,8 and the FDA has since approved an expanded age indication.3

"Patients often come in asking for LASIK by name. My job is to measure their eyes and tell them honestly which procedure will give them the best long-term result."

DR. ROBERT J. WEINSTOCK · DRAFT QUOTE FOR DR. WEINSTOCK'S APPROVAL

## What if you're over 45?

Around your mid-40s, the eye's natural lens starts losing its ability to focus up close, a condition called presbyopia. Neither LASIK nor ICL stops that, and the FDA notes that people who used reading glasses before LASIK may still need them afterward.7

For many people in this stage, a lens-based procedure such as Clear Lens Exchange can address near and distance vision together and remove the chance of a future cataract.

## Questions to ask your surgeon

  * Which procedure do my measurements support, and why?
  * How many of these procedures have you performed with this laser or lens?7
  * Will I still need reading glasses, now or later?
  * What does recovery look like, and how many follow-up visits will I have?

After LASIK, expect to see your doctor within the first 24 to 48 hours and at regular visits after that.6

## Frequently asked questions

Is EVO ICL better than LASIK?

Neither is better for everyone. LASIK is a strong option for many people with stable prescriptions and healthy corneas, while EVO ICL is often a better fit for higher prescriptions, thin corneas or dry eye concerns.

Can EVO ICL be removed?

Yes. Because the lens is placed inside the eye without removing corneal tissue, it can be removed or exchanged if needed.

Will I need reading glasses after LASIK or ICL?

Possibly. Both procedures correct distance vision but do not stop presbyopia, the age-related loss of near focus that usually begins in the mid-40s.

How do I know which one I qualify for?

A full evaluation measures your prescription, corneal thickness and shape, and the internal dimensions of your eye. Those measurements determine which procedure is safe and effective for you.

## Sources

  1. UnitedHealthcare Newsroom. 5 tips to consider before laser eye surgery (citing FDA approvals). <https://newsroom.uhc.com/health/laser-vision-correction.html>
  2. Optometry Times. FDA approves STAAR Surgical's EVO Visian ICL for myopia. March 28, 2022. <https://optometrytimes.com/view/fda-approves-staar-surgical-s-evo-visian-icl-for-myopia>
  3. Eyes On Eyecare Glance. FDA approves expanded age indication for STAAR's EVO/EVO+ Visian ICLs. February 19, 2026. <https://glance.eyesoneyecare.com/stories/2026-02-19/fda-approves-expanded-age-indication-for-staar-s-evo-evo-visian-icls/>
  4. Healio. FDA approves EVO Visian lens. April 12, 2022. <https://www.healio.com/news/ophthalmology/20220412/fda-approves-evo-visian-lens>
  5. EyeWorld, ASCRS. FDA approves new ICL. April 1, 2022. <https://www.eyeworld.org/?p=11499>
  6. U.S. Food and Drug Administration. LASIK: What should I expect before, during, and after surgery? <https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/lasik/what-should-i-expect-during-and-after-surgery>

# 7 Signs You May Need Cataract Surgery | Dr. Robert Weinstock, Largo FL

Source: https://proposals.localairegistry.com/weinstock/articles/signs-you-need-cataract-surgery/
Updated: 2026-11-19

Cataracts

# 7 Signs It May Be Time for Cataract Surgery

Cataracts creep in slowly, so most people adapt without noticing. Here are the seven signs a cataract may be affecting your life, and how to know when surgery makes sense.

**By[Robert J. Weinstock, MD](https://proposals.localairegistry.com/weinstock/dr-robert-weinstock/)**Board-certified cataract & refractive surgeon · Largo, FL

**Published** November 17, 2026**Medically reviewed** November 17, 20266 min read

Stock photo.

**On this page**

  1. What is a cataract?
  2. The 7 signs to watch for
  3. When is it time for surgery?
  4. What cataract surgery involves
  5. FAQ
  6. Sources

**Key takeaways**

  * A cataract is a clouding of the eye's natural lens, and it usually develops slowly.
  * Common signs include blurry or dim vision, glare and halos, poor night vision and faded colors.
  * Surgery is usually the right time when blurry vision gets in the way of everyday life.
  * Cataract surgery replaces the cloudy lens with a clear artificial lens, and the right lens can also reduce your need for glasses.

## What is a cataract?

A cataract is a clouding of the lens inside your eye, which is normally clear.1 The lens sits behind the colored part of your eye and focuses light, so as it clouds, the image you see turns blurry, dim and washed out.

Age is the biggest risk factor. By age 80, more than half of all Americans either have a cataract or have had cataract surgery.2 Diabetes, long-term steroid use, eye injuries, previous eye surgery and years of sun exposure can all speed things up.1

## The 7 signs to watch for

Because cataracts usually grow slowly, early changes are easy to miss.3 These are the signs eye surgeons hear about most often:

### 1\. Cloudy, blurry or dim vision

It can feel like looking through a smudged or foggy window, even with clean glasses.3

### 2\. Glare and halos around lights

Headlights, lamps or sunlight may seem too bright, or you may see rings around lights.2

### 3\. Trouble seeing at night

Night driving is often the first thing people start avoiding.2

### 4\. Colors that look faded or yellowed

Whites can look dingy and blues can look dull, a change many patients only notice after surgery.3

### 5\. Frequent prescription changes

If your glasses or contacts never seem quite right for long, a changing lens may be the reason.3

### 6\. Double vision in one eye

Seeing a ghost image with one eye closed can be a sign of a cataract.3

### 7\. Needing more light to read

If you keep turning up the lamp or reaching for a flashlight to read menus, the lens may be letting in less light.4

**See a doctor right away** if you notice a sudden shower of floaters, flashes of light or a curtain over part of your vision. Those are usually not cataract symptoms and can signal a retinal emergency.

Questions about your own eyes?

Book a consultation with Dr. Weinstock in Largo.

[Book a Consultation](https://proposals.localairegistry.com/weinstock/#contact)

## When is it time for surgery?

There is rarely a rush. In general, cataract surgery makes sense when blurry vision starts to get in the way of everyday life, like driving, reading, working or enjoying hobbies.1

A comprehensive eye exam is the only way to confirm a cataract and rule out other conditions that cause similar symptoms.1

"The question I ask patients is simple: what are you no longer doing because of your eyes? That answer usually tells us when the time is right."

DR. ROBERT J. WEINSTOCK · DRAFT QUOTE FOR DR. WEINSTOCK'S APPROVAL

## What cataract surgery involves

Cataract surgery removes the cloudy natural lens and, in most cases, replaces it with a clear artificial lens called an intraocular lens (IOL).5 It is an outpatient procedure.

Today's lens options can do more than restore clarity. With the right lens, cataract surgery can also correct nearsightedness, farsightedness or astigmatism, which means less dependence on glasses afterward. Dr. Weinstock has served as a principal investigator on dozens of clinical studies of new intraocular lenses and surgical systems, so lens selection is a big part of every consultation.

Wondering what it costs? Read [what Medicare covers for cataract surgery](https://proposals.localairegistry.com/weinstock/articles/does-medicare-cover-cataract-surgery/).

## Frequently asked questions

Can cataracts go away on their own?

No. A cataract does not clear up on its own. Brighter lighting and updated glasses can help for a while, but surgery is the only way to remove a cataract.

Is there harm in waiting?

For most people, waiting is safe as long as vision is not interfering with daily life or safety, such as driving. Your eye surgeon can tell you whether waiting makes sense for your eyes.

Does cataract surgery hurt?

Cataract surgery is performed with numbing drops, and most patients describe feeling pressure rather than pain.

Can I get rid of my glasses after cataract surgery?

Many patients can reduce their need for glasses by choosing a lens that also corrects nearsightedness, farsightedness or astigmatism. Your consultation will cover which lenses fit your eyes and lifestyle.

About Dr. Weinstock

## A surgeon who helps shape _the field he practices  in_

Robert J. Weinstock, MD, is a board-certified ophthalmologist who specializes in cataract and refractive surgery, including laser cataract surgery, premium and light adjustable lens implants, LASIK, EVO ICL and refractive lens exchange. He practices at The Eye Institute of West Florida in Largo and Clearwater, where he is Medical Director, and serves as Regional Medical Director for EyeCare Partners.

He trained in cataract and refractive surgery under his father, Stephen M. Weinstock, MD, completing his fellowship at The Eye Institute of West Florida in 2002. Since then he has served as principal investigator on 32 clinical studies of new lenses, lasers and surgical systems, written 14 textbook chapters, and lectured at major meetings including ASCRS, the American Academy of Ophthalmology and AECOS.

He has written textbook chapters on microincisional and 3D heads-up digital cataract surgery, helped develop TrueVision 3D surgical visualization, and teaches the next generation as Fellowship Director at The Eye Institute of West Florida and Ophthalmology Rotation Director for Evara Health residents.

He has written more than 200 published articles and given more than 500 lectures internationally. Outside the operating room, he lives in Tampa Bay with his wife and three sons, and spends his free time fishing, freediving, spearfishing and snowboarding.

Questions

## About _Dr.  Weinstock_

Is Dr. Robert Weinstock board certified?

Yes. Dr. Weinstock has been a Diplomate of the American Board of Ophthalmology since 2003. He also holds American Board of Eye Surgery sub-specialty certifications in refractive surgery (LASIK) and cataract and implant surgery, both earned in 2007.

Where did Dr. Weinstock train?

He earned his MD at The Chicago Medical School, completed his ophthalmology residency at Saint Louis University School of Medicine, where he served as Clinical and Administrative Chief Resident, and completed a fellowship in cataract and refractive surgery at The Eye Institute of West Florida.

Where does Dr. Weinstock see patients?

Dr. Weinstock sees patients at The Eye Institute of West Florida in Largo, with an additional office in Clearwater. He performs surgery at the Largo Ambulatory Surgery Center, where he is Medical Director.

What procedures does Dr. Weinstock specialize in?

He specializes in cataract and refractive surgery, including laser cataract surgery, premium and light adjustable lens implants, LASIK, EVO ICL and refractive lens exchange.

Is Dr. Weinstock involved in research and teaching?

Yes. He has served on 42 clinical studies, 32 of them as principal investigator, written 14 textbook chapters and is an Assistant Clinical Professor of Ophthalmology at the University of South Florida Eye Institute.

What awards has Dr. Weinstock received?

His honors include Newsweek's America's Best Eye Doctors (2022), Ocular Surgery News Premier Surgeon 300 (2016), Castle Connolly Top Doctor (2017), the American Academy of Ophthalmology Achievement Award (2009) and Tampa Bay Metro Magazine Top Doctors in ten editions from 2013 to 2026. He is also President-Elect of the American-European Congress of Ophthalmic Surgery (AECOS).

Laser Cataract Surgery

## Cataracts Are Common.  
_Cloudy Vision Doesn't Have to Be._

Cataracts can make the world look dim, blurry and full of glare, especially at night. With laser cataract surgery and advanced lens implants, Dr. Weinstock removes the cloudy lens and can also correct nearsightedness, farsightedness or astigmatism, so you can get back to driving, reading and the things you love.

Questions

## Answers _before you  visit_

How do I know if I need cataract surgery?

Common signs include cloudy or dim vision, glare and halos around lights, faded colors and trouble driving at night. A comprehensive eye exam with Dr. Weinstock is the only way to know for sure.

Am I a candidate for LASIK?

Good LASIK candidates are adults with a stable prescription and healthy corneas. If your corneas are thin or your prescription is high, EVO ICL or Clear Lens Exchange may be a better fit. Your consultation will tell you which.

Does Medicare cover cataract surgery?

Medicare and most insurance plans typically cover medically necessary cataract surgery. Our team reviews your coverage, and any cost for premium lens options, before your procedure.

Where is Weinstock Vision located?

Our main office is at 1225 West Bay Drive in Largo, Florida, and we serve patients from Clearwater, St. Petersburg and Tampa. Surgery is performed at the Largo Ambulatory Surgery Center, where Dr. Weinstock is Medical Director.

What are your office hours?

We are open Monday through Friday, 8 AM to 5 PM, and closed Saturday and Sunday.

Who will perform my surgery?

Dr. Robert J. Weinstock, a board-certified, fellowship-trained cataract and refractive surgeon named one of Newsweek's America's Best Eye Doctors.
